title: 3XOR: all triples vs a Patricia trie (deterministic quadratic)
problem_statement: Given an integer w >= 1 and a tuple of n integers a_0..a_{n-1} in [0, 2^w), find indices i < j < k with a_i XOR a_j XOR a_k = 0 (bitwise exclusive or), or report that none exist (output None). Any such triple is a correct answer; different algorithms may return different triples.

input.size_measure: n words of w bits each (n w bits). Word operations (XOR, AND with a mask, comparison) are counted at unit cost. The V1 battery uses w from 1 to 64; the V2 family has w = log2(n) + 1.

algorithms.name: all triples
algorithms.idea: For every pair i < j compute t = a_i XOR a_j once, then scan k > j for a_k = t; return the first hit.
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^3) in the worst case. Exactly, on every instance without a solution (the V2 family is one): C(n, 2) XORs and C(n, 3) equality tests, C(n, 2) + C(n, 3) = C(n + 1, 3) = (n^3 - n)/6 word operations (the middle loop runs once per pair, the inner loop once per triple; Pascal's rule sums the two binomials). With a solution it stops at the first hit.
algorithms.correctness: Exhaustive: a_i XOR a_j XOR a_k = 0 iff a_k = a_i XOR a_j, and every triple i < j < k is tested.

shape.note: The V2 family exists for n = 2^(w-1); the count equals (n^3 - n)/6 from n = 1 on (0 at n = 1), so the grid starts at 1 and keeps the default holdout of 4 with 10 terms.

algorithms.name: Patricia trie
algorithms.idea: Handle the solutions that contain a 0 (0,0,0 and x,x,0) by a zero scan and the multiplicities of a Patricia trie over the nonzero values. For three distinct nonzero values, use the trie to list a XOR x over all distinct nonzero x in ascending order in linear time for each a (take the right child first where a has the node's bit), and merge that list with the distinct values in ascending order (the trie's leaf order): a common value c = a XOR b is a solution. This follows the idea of the deterministic quadratic algorithm of Dietzfelbinger, Schlag & Walzer 2018; the code here is an independent implementation.
algorithms.pseudocode:
Z = indices i with a_i == 0 (n equality tests)
if |Z| >= 3: return the first three indices of Z
build a Patricia trie over the indices of the nonzero values: split a group by bit w-1, w-2, ..., 0;
  no split at a bit: skip the bit; split: branching node (bit, left = bit 0, right = bit 1);
  a group of size 1 is a leaf; a group that runs out of bits is a leaf of equal values
if Z nonempty and some leaf holds >= 2 indices (a value x != 0 twice): return two of them and Z[0], in increasing order
D = one index per leaf, left to right (distinct nonzero values, ascending)
for a in D:
  X = in-order walk, right child first at every branching node whose bit is set in a, emitting a XOR x per leaf x
  merge X with D (both strictly ascending): on a common value c = a XOR b return the indices of a, b, c in increasing order
return None
algorithms.time_complexity: O(n^2 + n w) word operations; Theta(n^2) in the worst case when log2(n) + 1 <= w = O(n) (n distinct odd-weight words exist there and form a no-instance whose n rounds make n XORs each; exact count on the V2 family). The zero scan is n comparisons, the build at most n w bit tests (each index is tested once per bit until its group is a singleton), and each of the |D| <= n rounds costs O(|D|): |D| - 1 bit tests at branching nodes, |D| XORs and a merge of at most 2|D| - 1 steps. Exactly, on the V2 family (all w-bit words of odd Hamming weight, n = 2^(w-1), no solution): 7n^2 + 2n log2(n) - 3n operations. Derivation: n zero comparisons; the build tests every word once at each of the bits w-1..1 (a group fixed on its top bits holds all suffixes of one parity, 2^(r-1) words for r remaining bits, and splits at the next bit while r >= 2; at r = 1 it is a single word), n(w - 1) = n log2(n) bit tests of 2 operations each (AND, truth test), and the trie has n leaves and n - 1 branching nodes; per a: 2(n - 1) for the bit tests at branching nodes, n XORs, and the merge: {a XOR x} is the set of even-weight words, which interleaves with the odd-weight words (each pair 2t, 2t + 1 holds one of each), so the merge consumes every word up to 2^w - 2, 2n - 1 steps of one equality test and one less-than test, 4n - 2; per a 7n - 4. Total n + 2n log2(n) + n(7n - 4).
algorithms.space_complexity: Theta(n) words: the build keeps an explicit stack of pending index groups, and these groups are disjoint subsets of the n indices, so together with the current group they hold at most n indices, plus at most min(n - 1, w) node markers. After the build, Theta(n) words: the trie (at most n leaves and n - 1 branching nodes), the leaf index lists, and one list of |D| pairs per round.
algorithms.correctness: Case analysis. Let a_i XOR a_j XOR a_k = 0 with i, j, k distinct. If two of the values are equal, say a_i = a_j, then a_k = a_i XOR a_j = 0; if all three are equal, then a_i = a_i XOR a_i XOR a_i = 0. If the three values are pairwise distinct, none is 0, since a_k = 0 would give a_i = a_j (and symmetrically). So every solution is (0, 0, 0) at three zero indices, or (x, x, 0) with x != 0, or three pairwise distinct nonzero values. Step 1 finds the first kind whenever 0 occurs >= 3 times. Otherwise 0 occurs at most twice, so a solution with a 0 has exactly one 0 and two equal nonzero values: step 3 finds it iff 0 occurs and some leaf holds two indices. Otherwise only the third kind is possible. Trie order: two leaves x != y with lowest common ancestor v (bit b) agree on every bit above b (on a skipped bit all members of the group agree; at a branching ancestor above v they took the same side) and differ at b, with x in the left (bit 0) subtree; so x < y, and the left-to-right leaf order is ascending. a XOR x and a XOR y also agree above b and differ at b, and a XOR x < a XOR y iff bit b of a is 0, which is exactly when the walk visits the left subtree of v first; hence the walk lists the a XOR x in ascending order, strictly since x -> a XOR x is injective. Merge: two strictly ascending lists; whenever the head of one list is smaller than the head of the other, it is smaller than every remaining element of the other list, so it cannot be a common value and may be dropped; therefore if a common value exists, the merge finds one. A common value c = a XOR b with b, c in D: c != 0 forces a != b; c = a would force b = 0 and c = b would force a = 0, both excluded since 0 is not in D; so the representatives of a, b, c are three distinct indices with a XOR b XOR c = 0. Conversely, for a solution of the third kind with values a, b, c, the round for a finds c = a XOR b (or another common value) in both lists. If no round finds one, no solution exists.

shape.note: The count equals 7n^2 + 2n log2(n) - 3n from n = 1 on (4 at n = 1), so the grid starts at 1: 12 terms for an order-3 recurrence with the default holdout of 4.

relationship: Worst cases: Theta(n^3) -> O(n^2 + n w) word operations, i.e. Theta(n^3) -> Theta(n^2) for log2(n) + 1 <= w = O(n). Both algorithms are deterministic and exact. The entry makes no claim about the fastest known algorithm for 3XOR or about lower bounds.

sources.authors: Dietzfelbinger, M.; Schlag, P.; Walzer, S.

verification.method: V1: the validator runs n = 0..8, 10, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 100, 150, 300 and 600, 8 instances per size (160 instances, 312 implementation runs; all triples up to n = 300, the Patricia trie on every size). By the oracle, 79 instances have a solution and 81 do not; n <= 2 never has one, and both answers occur at 15 of the 17 sizes n >= 3 (not at n = 4: 8 no, and n = 300: 8 yes). The instances mix five kinds: words of floor(log2 n) + 1..3 bits (mostly yes); random 64-bit words (no) with a planted triple half of the time; odd-Hamming-weight words (always no); duplicates and 0..3 zeros on a pool of odd-weight words, which isolates the solutions (0, 0, 0) and (x, x, 0); and words of 1..4 bits. Both implementations agree on whether a triple exists, and every output passes check, which is independent of both: a returned triple must be a tuple of three ints (bool, float, str and lists are rejected) with 0 <= i < j < k < n and XOR 0; None is judged by a hash-based Theta(n^2) pair scan with a Counter that discounts the pair's own indices (as in the 3SUM harness). experiments/2026-10-06i_three_xor.py adds 525 instances for both implementations (n = 0..12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 48, 64, 100, 150; 248 yes, 277 no; 0 disagreements, 0 check failures) and 20 for the trie alone (n = 300, 600; 14 yes; 0 failures), and runs an oracle control: 2977 deliberately wrong outputs on 360 instances, all rejected (0 accepted, 0 undecided): a triple with nonzero XOR 290, a repeated index whose XOR is 0 ((i, i, z) or (z, i, i) with value 0 at z) 126, unsorted indices 348, negative indices that alias a real solution through Python's negative indexing 174, out of range 320, wrong arity (pairs, 4-tuples, a correct triple as a list) 771, bool entries 206 plus (False, True, k) on instances where values[0] ^ values[1] ^ values[k] = 0 94, float 174, str 174, None on a yes-instance 174, a triple on a no-instance 126; the 720 outputs of the two implementations were all accepted. V2 (exact counts, measure 'reported'): generate_scaling(n, rng) with n = 2^(w-1) gives all w-bit words of odd Hamming weight (w = log2(n) + 1), shuffled by rng, as CountingInt values; CountingInt counts ^, &, |, >>, <<, the six comparisons and truth tests on input values and on values computed from them, returns CountingInt for bitwise results and has no hash. It is a no-instance (three odd-weight words XOR to an odd-weight word), so neither algorithm stops early, and the implementations are the V1 code unchanged. All triples: exactly (n^3 - n)/6 = C(n, 2) XORs + C(n, 3) equality tests, confirmed in total and per kind for n = 1, 2, 4, ..., 512; fit on n = 16..512: alpha = 1.000 (tol 0.02); rivals n**2 (1.500), n**3*log(n) (0.929) and n**4 (0.750) rejected. Patricia trie: exactly 7n^2 + 2n log2(n) - 3n, per kind n^2 XORs, n log2(n) + n(n - 1) ANDs and as many truth tests, 4n^2 - n comparisons, confirmed for n = 1, 2, 4, ..., 2048 (and the trie of the family has n leaves and n - 1 branching nodes, n = 1..1024); fit on n = 32..2048: alpha = 1.000; rivals n**3 (0.664), n**2*log(n) (0.911) and n*log(n) (1.678) rejected. The log-factor diagnostic is resolved in both fits (alpha vs cost*log n / cost/log n: 0.928 / 1.084 and 0.914 / 1.104). The bare leading terms would also fit (n**3: 1.000311, n**2: 0.996615; experiment, information only); the cost expressions are the exact closed forms (RESEARCH_LOG RL-062). The counts are functions of n alone: three other shuffles per n = 1..256 give identical counts. Shape diagnostic (tools/validate.py --scaling -v): all triples [doubling n = 1..512, 10 terms] MATCH n^3, (log n)^0 (C-finite order 2, 6 terms used, 10 checked); Patricia trie [doubling n = 1..2048, 12 terms] MATCH n^2, (log n)^0 (C-finite order 3, 8 terms used, 12 checked). Cross-version: the experiment prints every V2 and shape-grid count series with the validator's seeding; CPython 3.14.2 and 3.12.10 print identical output with SHA-256 d38397740dfacbacb07d2e12ffba034a4ed2b6b3f1bdcdf411e23343080ef9cb. No counted operation runs inside a CPython built-in (RESEARCH_LOG RL-069 does not apply).

caveats: Word operations on w-bit words (XOR, AND with a mask, comparison) are counted at unit cost, as on a word RAM; the bit complexity is larger by a factor of up to w. The Patricia trie costs O(n^2 + n w): building the trie takes up to n w bit tests, so the Theta(n^2) bound needs w = O(n), and for w much larger than n the build dominates; its lower half is stated only for w >= log2(n) + 1, where n distinct odd-weight words form a no-instance with n rounds of n XORs each. The V2 family has w = log2(n) + 1, where the build contributes the lower-order term 2n log2(n). Theta(n^3) is the worst case of all triples, reached on every instance without a solution; on yes-instances both algorithms stop at the first triple they find. Counted: every operation on an input value or on a value computed from one (XOR, AND, comparisons, truth tests). Not counted: loop control, index arithmetic and index comparisons on plain integers, list appends, isinstance tests, the allocation of tuples and trie nodes, the mask 1 << bit built from a plain bit position, and the size parameter w. These are of the same order as the counted operations: all triples makes one inner-loop iteration per equality test and one middle-loop iteration per XOR; on the V2 family the Patricia trie makes, per round, 2n - 1 node visits (n leaves and n - 1 branching nodes, each a stack pop and an isinstance test; n leaf tuples are allocated) and 2n - 1 merge iterations, against 7n - 4 counted operations. As one overall measure, sys.settrace counts 2.049 executed source lines per counted operation for all triples and 3.009 for the trie at n = 64 (experiment, part a). No counted operation runs inside a CPython built-in: neither implementation calls sorted, min or max or puts input values into a dict or set or hashes them; the Counter is used only by the oracle, outside the measurement. Both implementations assume values in [0, 2^w); the trie looks only at bits w-1..0. The entry makes no claim about the fastest known algorithm for 3XOR and states no lower bound.
notes: 3XOR is studied alongside 3SUM in fine-grained complexity (Jafargholi & Viola 2016). Relative in the dataset: three-sum-cubic-vs-quadratic, the additive analogue (all triples vs sorting with two pointers). Here the trie takes the place of sorting: XOR with a fixed a permutes the leaves of the trie by swapping the two subtrees at every branching node whose bit a has, so the list a XOR D comes out sorted in linear time for each a, with no sorting step. All triples returns the lexicographically first solution (i, j, k); the trie algorithm returns the first solution its case order and merge meet, so the two outputs may differ, and V1 compares only whether a triple was found.
